results.authors: Montalban X, Lebrun-Frenay C, Oh J, et al.
results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve). The optic nerve can be shown by MRI, OCT or VEP. The kappa free light chain index is accepted alongside CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands. The central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions are supporting MRI markers.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria

results.authors: Wattjes MP, Ciccarelli O, Reich DS, et al.
results.key_findings: Diagnostic MRI should include the brain with 3D FLAIR, T2 and pre- and post-gadolinium T1, and the spinal cord with at least two sagittal sequences, ideally in the same session.
results.title: 2021 MAGNIMS-CMSC-NAIMS consensus recommendations on the use of MRI in patients with multiple sclerosis

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
Do not attribute the current leg symptoms or the earlier leg episode to lumbar radiculopathy: the T10 sensory level, brisk reflexes, Babinski sign and Lhermitte sign localise to the spinal cord
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord and right optic nerve: five regions, so no separate DIT is required).

Exclude urinary tract infection (urinalysis and culture) before steroids, then give high-dose methylprednisolone for the disabling relapse (right optic neuritis 20/60 with paraparesis and bladder urgency): IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days as an inpatient or oral 500 mg daily for 5 days; avoid ibuprofen during the course or add a proton pump inhibitor; consider plasma exchange if severe deficits do not respond.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 8 months, enhancing brain, optic nerve and cord lesions, lesions in 5 of 5 regions), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, check full blood count with lymphocyte count, liver function, HBsAg and anti-HBc, hepatitis C and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive), and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before treatment starts
Measure the post-void residual for the urinary urgency: offer an antimuscarinic if the residual is low, and intermittent self-catheterisation if it is above 100 mL.

Normal ACE (27 U/L) and calcium, no leptomeningeal enhancement on brain or spine MRI, no systemic features
B12 520 pg/mL and normal MCV; focal enhancing cord, brain and optic nerve lesions are not explained by B12 deficiency

CSF VDRL nonreactive; no risk history or systemic signs
No encephalopathy; two attacks eight months apart; discrete ovoid lesions rather than large confluent ones

key_clinical_evidence: Subacute painful right optic neuritis (acuity 20/60, right RAPD, red desaturation, normal disc) with an enhancing swollen 12 mm retrobulbar segment of the right optic nerve and a prolonged right P100 (124 ms).

Concurrent myelopathy: right-predominant spastic paraparesis, right Babinski sign, T10 pinprick level, urinary urgency and Lhermitte sign, matched by the right dorsolateral C3-C4 and dorsal-column T6-T7 lesions.

DIS: 5 of 5 regions: periventricular (ovoid and callososeptal lesions), juxtacortical (left frontal), infratentorial (right middle cerebellar peduncle), spinal cord (C3-C4, T6-T7), optic nerve (right). With five regions no separate DIT or CSF is needed; enhancing and non-enhancing lesions also coexist.
Prior attack 8 months ago: 3 weeks of numbness in both legs from the knees down with difficulty walking, attributed elsewhere to lumbar radiculopathy without imaging.

AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative by cell-based assay, short peripheral cord lesions and five CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (kFLC index 24.7) argue against NMOSD and MOGAD; ACE, B12, ANA and CSF VDRL are normal.
Low 25-OH vitamin D (24 ng/mL) despite supplementation is a risk factor and comorbidity; it does not explain the lesions.

patient.history_present_illness: This 31-year-old left-handed woman of East Asian descent presents to the neurology inpatient service with a two-week history of progressive painful vision loss in the right eye and worsening bilateral lower extremity weakness. The symptoms began approximately 14 days ago when she noticed a dull, aching pain behind her right eye that worsened with eye movements. Over the following three to four days, she developed blurry vision in that eye, initially describing it as looking through frosted glass, which progressively worsened to the point that she could barely read her computer screen with the right eye alone. She also noticed that colors appeared washed out in the right eye compared to the left. Around the same time, she began experiencing heaviness and stiffness in both legs, more pronounced on the right side, with occasional tripping when walking. She reports that her legs feel clumsy, particularly going up stairs, and she has stumbled several times at home. She endorses a band-like tightness around her mid-abdomen that started approximately ten days ago. Additionally, she has noticed an electric shock-like sensation running down her spine into her arms and legs when she bends her neck forward. She reports increased urinary urgency over the past week, though she denies frank incontinence. On further questioning, she recalls a distinct episode approximately eight months ago when she experienced numbness and tingling in both legs from the knees down, accompanied by difficulty walking, which lasted about three weeks and then gradually improved. She saw a primary care physician at the time who attributed her symptoms to possible lumbar radiculopathy and prescribed ibuprofen. No imaging was performed during that episode. She denies any recent infections, fevers, rashes, joint pain, oral ulcers, or Raynaud phenomenon. She has not traveled recently and denies any tick exposures.
